node.title: Cancer cell survival without oxidative phosphorylation
node.canonical_question: Can cancer cells survive without mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation?
node.summary: Many cancer cells rely primarily on aerobic glycolysis (the Warburg effect) rather than oxidative phosphorylation, even when oxygen is available. Most can survive with greatly reduced OxPhos, but mitochondria remain important for biosynthetic precursors and redox balance. Some cancers are still highly OxPhos-dependent.

sections.title: The Warburg effect: glycolysis in the presence of oxygen
sections.content: Normal cells use oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) when oxygen is available, because it produces far more ATP per glucose than glycolysis. In 1924, Otto Warburg observed that cancer cells often do the opposite: they consume glucose and produce lactate at high rates even when oxygen is plentiful. This is called aerobic glycolysis or the Warburg effect. Because cancer cells favour glycolysis, they are less dependent on OxPhos for energy, and many can survive — and even proliferate — when OxPhos is severely impaired.

sections.title: Why cancer cells tolerate reduced OxPhos
sections.content: Aerobic glycolysis produces only about 2 ATP per glucose, compared with roughly 30 from full oxidative phosphorylation. Cancer cells compensate by greatly increasing glucose uptake — often absorbing glucose 10 to 100 times faster than the surrounding normal tissue. The high glycolytic flux supplies enough ATP and, importantly, provides carbon skeletons for building nucleotides, amino acids, and lipids needed for rapid cell division. So reduced OxPhos is not a fatal flaw for a cancer cell; it is often a metabolic trade-off that favours biosynthesis over energy efficiency.

sections.title: Mitochondria still matter in cancer
sections.content: Even cancer cells that are highly glycolytic still rely on mitochondria for functions beyond ATP production. The Krebs cycle supplies biosynthetic intermediates (oxaloacetate for amino acids, citrate for fatty acid synthesis). The electron transport chain is needed to regenerate NAD+ and maintain redox balance. Mitochondria also regulate apoptosis: release of cytochrome c from the mitochondrial intermembrane space can trigger cell death. Some anti-cancer drugs work precisely by targeting mitochondrial function in cancer cells, exploiting the fact that cancer cell mitochondria are in an unusual metabolic state.

sections.title: Variation across cancer types
sections.content: Not all cancers are equally glycolytic. Some, including certain leukaemias, lymphomas, and some solid tumours in low-glucose environments, remain highly dependent on OxPhos. Research has shown that blocking OxPhos with drugs such as metformin or IACS-010759 can slow growth in these OxPhos-dependent cancers. There is also evidence that cancer cells can switch between glycolysis and OxPhos depending on nutrient availability, oxygen levels, and the demands of the tumour microenvironment.

sections.title: Connection to the main lesson
sections.content: This topic is a direct extension of the core ideas about OxPhos and cellular respiration covered in the parent lesson. The electron transport chain, proton gradient, and ATP synthase all work the same way in cancer cells as in normal cells — the difference is that many cancer cells downregulate their reliance on this machinery and upregulate glycolysis instead. Understanding the Warburg effect shows that the relative use of these pathways can shift dramatically depending on cell state, and that mitochondria serve roles beyond simply making ATP.

rendering.explanation: Cancer cells can often survive with very little oxidative phosphorylation. Many of them prefer to break glucose down by glycolysis even when oxygen is available — a quirk first noticed by Otto Warburg about a century ago. Glycolysis yields far less ATP per glucose, but cancer cells compensate by taking up massive amounts of glucose, and they gain a bonus: the process produces raw materials for building new cell components, which suits rapidly dividing tumour cells well. That said, cancer cells cannot completely abandon their mitochondria. The mitochondria still run the Krebs cycle to make building blocks for DNA, proteins, and fats, and they still regulate whether the cell lives or dies. Some cancers are actually very dependent on oxidative phosphorylation, and researchers are now testing drugs that target that dependency.
